title: Leveling Up Through the React Lifecycle
markdown:
> Extra! Extra! Don't walk by without reading!

As of this writing React has shipped v16.12.0, and the lifecycle is the little buddy you meet every day in production. Unfortunately, the buddy changed.

## Why it changed

Before v16.3, updates in React were synchronous, which could hurt performance.

Example: a huge module nests many components. Once the top-level `render` runs, every nested `render` runs in turn down to the leaves. That can freeze the main thread.

To fix this, React introduced Fiber. The idea is time-sliced work. One update splits into two phases: Reconciliation and Commit.

In Reconciliation, Fiber figures out which DOM needs updating — and this phase can be interrupted. In Commit, the DOM updates run to completion and will not be interrupted.

Those phases map to different lifecycle methods:

**Phase 1**

- componentWillMount
- componentWillReceiveProps
- shouldComponentUpdate
- componentWillUpdate

**Phase 2**

- componentDidMount
- componentDidUpdate
- componentWillUnmount

See this demo: Fiber vs Stack Demo

## Before and after

Before:

![image]()

Now (v16.3):

![image]()

Comparing the two diagrams, React deprecated:

- componentWillMount
- componentWillReceiveProps
- componentWillUpdate

For compatibility, `UNSAFE_componentWillMount`, `UNSAFE_componentWillReceiveProps`, and `UNSAFE_componentWillUpdate` were added. Old and new names both work for a while, but old names warn in red in development and are removed for good in React 17.

New methods:

- getDerivedStateFromProps
- getSnapshotBeforeUpdate

## Lifecycle by phase

Below is a pass through mount, update, and unmount.

![image]()

### constructor

Runs first. Use it for setup such as initial state; if you do not need that, you do not need a constructor for a React component.

### getDerivedStateFromProps

When the component is created, this replaces `componentWillMount()`. When new props arrive, it replaces `componentWillReceiveProps()` and `componentWillUpdate()`.

```javascript
static getDerivedStateFromProps(nextProps, prevState)
```

In v16.3 it was not called after every re-render; from v16.4 it runs on re-renders as well. That means even if props did not change, a parent re-render can still trigger it on the child.

### componentWillMount / UNSAFE_componentWillMount (going away)

Some people put data fetches here to get data faster for the first paint. In reality, no request is faster than the first render — and because of Fiber, this method may run more than once, which means the API may be hit more than once. It is fully removed after v17.

### componentDidMount

Called after mount, once per mount. Safe place for refs and real DOM access. You can also start async requests here and `setState` in their callbacks.

### componentWillReceiveProps / UNSAFE_componentWillReceiveProps (going away)

Replaced by `getDerivedStateFromProps`.

### shouldComponentUpdate

After every `setState`, React asks `shouldComponentUpdate` whether to re-render. Default is `true` (re-render). Return `false` to skip. In complex apps some data changes do not affect the UI — decide here and save render work.

### componentWillUpdate

Again because of Fiber, recording DOM state here is no longer reliable.

### getSnapshotBeforeUpdate

Fires in the instant before DOM updates — a more accurate place than `componentWillUpdate` to snapshot DOM state.

### componentDidUpdate

After the first render you get `componentDidMount`; after later renders you get `componentDidUpdate`.

### componentWillUnmount

Called when the component unmounts. Events registered in `componentDidMount` usually get cleaned up here.

## Summary

Synchronous component updates caused performance issues and main-thread freezes, so Fiber re-implemented the core algorithm. Fiber also made some lifecycle methods run more than once, so those methods were retired and new ones introduced.

- Component lifecycle after React v16.3
